subsection: 2. Emigration, 1855–1914 and 1920–1966; restriction and regulation after 1920

notes.b: After the Famine emigration did not stop; it became a settled part of Irish rural life.
points: About 4 million people left Ireland in the six decades after the Famine; estimates vary, but the population fell to about 4.4 million by 1911.
The United States took about four out of five emigrants; Britain, Canada, Australia and New Zealand took most of the rest.
Emigrants were mostly young and single, aged roughly 15 to 30, and Ireland was unusual in Europe in sending about as many women as men; in some decades women outnumbered men.
Emigration was heaviest from the west and south-west, especially Connacht, Kerry, Cork and Clare, and from the 1880s Connacht had the highest rate.
After the Famine farms were no longer subdivided: one son inherited the holding (impartible inheritance) and one daughter received a dowry, so the other children had to emigrate or stay unmarried.
Late marriage, falling farm employment as land turned to cattle grazing, and the lack of industry outside north-east Ulster pushed young people out.
Agricultural depression and evictions in 1879–1882 caused a fresh surge of emigration, especially from the west.

notes.h: The journey and the American wake
points: The American wake was an all-night farewell gathering, with music, dancing, food and drink as well as keening, held on the night before an emigrant left, because most emigrants never came back.
Steamships replaced sail from the 1860s, cutting the Atlantic crossing from about six weeks to about ten days by the 1870s and making the voyage far safer.
Liners of the Cunard, White Star and other lines called at Queenstown (Cobh) and at Moville near Derry to pick up emigrants travelling steerage.
In New York emigrants landed at Castle Garden from 1855 and at Ellis Island from 1892; the first person processed at Ellis Island, on 1 January 1892, was Annie Moore from Cork.
Colonial governments in Australia and New Zealand paid or subsidised passages to attract settlers, so Irish emigration there was largely assisted, while emigration to America was paid for privately.
In the USA the Irish settled overwhelmingly in cities of the north-east and Midwest: New York, Boston, Philadelphia, Chicago and the mill and mining towns of New England and Pennsylvania.
Irish men mostly started as unskilled labourers on docks, railways, canals and building sites and in mines and factories, and many moved up into skilled trades, police forces and fire departments.
Irish women dominated domestic service in cities such as New York and Boston; the job gave board, lodging and wages that could be saved and sent home.
Irish Americans moved into city politics through the Democratic Party, and by 1900 the second generation was entering teaching, clerical work and the professions.
In Britain the Irish settled in Liverpool, Glasgow, London, Manchester and the industrial towns of Lancashire and west-central Scotland, working on the docks, in building, in mills and in mines.
In Australia the Irish made up about a quarter of the population of European origin, settling as farmers, labourers and gold-miners in New South Wales, Victoria and Queensland.
Emigrants' remittances: money and pre-paid tickets sent home by emigrants, amounting to tens of millions of pounds between the Famine and 1914.
Much of the money came from servant girls and labourers, who sent home a large share of their wages.
Remittances paid for the passages of younger brothers and sisters, so one emigrant could bring out a whole family over a few years.
Remittances also paid rent, shop debts and dowries and helped families keep their holdings, which made emigration a support for the rural economy as well as a drain on it.
The American letter, often containing dollars, was a regular event in western households, and it kept relatives informed of jobs and wages abroad.
Chain-emigration meant that new arrivals stayed with kin, found work through them, and settled in the same parishes, so emigrant communities reproduced the networks of home.

notes.h: Assimilation in the USA and Britain
points: Assimilation in the USA was helped by the English language, the Democratic Party, the Catholic parish and its schools, and the sheer size of the Irish community.
By the early 20th century Irish Americans had risen into city government, the Catholic hierarchy and the professions, and the second generation increasingly thought of itself as American.
In Britain the Irish remained more visible as a separate, mainly Catholic working-class group, and sectarian rivalry with Protestant workers was strong in Liverpool and Glasgow.
Irish emigrants to Britain after 1920 were close to home, often expected to return, and kept Irish citizenship, which slowed assimilation for the first generation.
Their British-born children usually assimilated quickly, often losing an Irish accent and identity, while Irish clubs, dance halls and parishes sustained it for those who wanted it.
Irish-speaking emigrants from the Gaeltacht lost the language within a generation abroad, in both the USA and Britain.
The Emergency Quota Act of 1921 limited immigrants of each nationality to 3 per cent of that nationality's foreign-born population in the 1910 US census.

The Immigration Act of 1924 (Johnson-Reed Act) set quotas at 2 per cent of each foreign-born group in the 1890 census, a base chosen to favour north-western Europeans over southern and eastern Europeans.
The Irish Free State received a quota of 28,567 a year from 1925, cut to 17,853 from 1929 when the national-origins formula took effect; Northern Ireland came under the British quota.
Irish emigration to the USA stayed substantial through the 1920s, often reaching the quota, so the quotas themselves did not end it.
The Great Depression after 1929 did: in the early 1930s more Irish people returned from the USA than went there.
From the 1930s Britain became the main destination, because there were no restrictions on Irish entry, jobs were close, and the fare was low.
The Irish state did not try to stop emigration; independent Ireland's governments saw it as a national shame but treated it as an economic problem they could not quickly solve.

notes.h: Regulation during the Second World War and after
points: During the Emergency (1939–1945) Irish people needed travel permits and identity documents to go to Britain, and both governments controlled who could travel.

Britain recruited Irish workers for war factories, building and farm work, and by 1945 well over 100,000 people from the Irish state had gone to work in Britain; tens of thousands more joined the British forces.
The British Nationality Act of 1948 and the Ireland Act of 1949 confirmed that Irish citizens in the United Kingdom were not treated as aliens and could live, work and vote there freely.

Post-war reconstruction created huge demand for labour in Britain: Irish men worked as navvies on roads, building sites and power stations, while Irish women trained as nurses in the new National Health Service (1948) or worked in factories and offices.
The Irish in Britain clustered in London (Kilburn, Camden Town, Cricklewood), Birmingham, Coventry, Luton, Manchester and Liverpool.

The US Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 abolished the national-origins quotas from 1968, replacing them with a system favouring family ties and skills, which made it harder for Irish people without American relatives to enter.

notes.h: The 1950s crisis and the Commission on Emigration
points: The government set up the Commission on Emigration and Other Population Problems in 1948, and it reported in 1954.

The Commission found that emigration was caused mainly by economic factors such as low incomes, unemployment and small farms, but also by the dullness of rural life and the wish for better living standards.
It accepted that emigration could not be ended quickly and recommended economic development and improved rural conditions rather than any ban on leaving.
Emigration peaked in the 1950s: about 400,000 people left the state between 1951 and 1961, most of them for Britain.
The 1961 census recorded the lowest population in the history of the state, about 2.8 million.
The Vanishing Irish (1953), a collection of essays edited by the American priest John A. O'Brien, warned that the Irish nation was dying out through emigration and late marriage.
The First Programme for Economic Expansion (1958) under Seán Lemass and T.K. Whitaker brought growth that cut emigration sharply in the 1960s.
Many young emigrants arrived in Britain with no training, and lived in lodging houses or navvy camps where hard drinking and long hours were common.
Signs and advertisements saying No Irish, No Blacks, No Dogs were reported in London lodging-house windows in the 1950s and 1960s.
Catholic chaplaincies, the Legion of Mary and the Irish Centres in Camden (1955) and other cities helped new arrivals find lodgings and work.
Irish dance halls such as the Galtymore in Cricklewood and the Gresham on the Holloway Road became centres of emigrant social life.
Navvy work was often arranged through subcontractors who paid cash in hand on the lump, leaving workers without insurance or job security.

notes.b: Domhnall (Dónall) Mac Amhlaigh (1926–1989) was an Irish-language writer whose diary of navvy life is the best-known first-hand account of 1950s emigration to Britain.
points: Born in Co. Galway in 1926 and raised largely in Co. Kilkenny, he served in the Irish Army's Irish-speaking battalion in Galway.
Facing unemployment when he left the army in 1951, he went to Northampton, England, first working as a hospital porter and then as a labourer on building sites and roads.
His diary of 1951 to 1957, Dialann Deoraí (An Exile's Diary), was published in 1960; Valentin Iremonger translated it as An Irish Navvy: The Diary of an Exile (1964).
It describes the work, the lodgings, the pubs and dance halls, homesickness, and the mixture of welcome and prejudice the Irish met in England.
He was a participant, not an observer: he lived the life he described and stayed in England for the rest of his life, dying in 1989 and being buried in Northampton.
He went on to write novels and short stories in Irish, including Schnitzer Ó Sé (1974) and Deoraithe (1986), and journalism for Irish newspapers.
Contemporaries in Ireland valued the diary as a frank picture of a life that official Ireland preferred not to discuss; it was later used as a school text.
Historians now treat it as a key source on the Irish in post-war Britain, showing a generation that worked, socialised and kept its identity in an Irish world inside English cities.
Safety valve versus drain: emigration relieved rural poverty and unemployment and brought in remittances, but it took the young and kept the population falling until 1961.
Opportunity versus exile: many emigrants gained better wages and lives, while others, as Mac Amhlaigh shows, felt themselves exiles doing the hardest work.
US restriction redirected rather than stopped emigration: Britain's open door absorbed the flow after the 1930s.
Contemporary view: churchmen and politicians spoke of the vanishing Irish and blamed modern attractions as well as poverty; the Commission of 1954 placed the cause in economic weakness.
Later view: historians such as Enda Delaney see emigration to Britain as a choice by individuals within family strategies, not simply as forced exile.

keyTerms.definition: Money and pre-paid tickets sent home by emigrants, which paid for further passages, rent and dowries and supported the rural economy.
Emigration in stages along family and parish networks, in which each emigrant paid for and housed the next.
The process by which emigrants and their children adopted the language, customs and identity of their new country; faster in the USA than among first-generation Irish in Britain.
The all-night farewell gathering held before an emigrant left, treated like a wake because most emigrants never returned.
The post-Famine custom by which one son inherited the whole farm, leaving his brothers and sisters to emigrate or stay single.
The first US law limiting immigration by nationality, to 3 per cent of each group's foreign-born population in the 1910 census.
The Johnson-Reed Act, which set quotas at 2 per cent of each group in the 1890 census and gave the Irish Free State 28,567 places a year.

keyTerms.term: Commission on Emigration and Other Population Problems
keyTerms.definition: The state inquiry of 1948 to 1954, which traced emigration to low incomes, unemployment and the poverty of rural life.
A manual labourer on roads, railways, canals and building sites, the typical job of Irish men in Britain.
The document Irish people needed to travel to Britain during the Second World War, when both governments controlled movement.

factCards.definition: By Domhnall Mac Amhlaigh, covering 1951 to 1957, published in 1960 and translated by Valentin Iremonger as An Irish Navvy (1964).
Born in Galway in 1926, an Irish Army soldier who went to Northampton in 1951, worked as a labourer, wrote in Irish and died there in 1989.

factCards.term: Irish Free State quota under the 1924 Act
factCards.definition: 28,567 a year from 1925, reduced to 17,853 from 1929 under the national-origins formula.

factCards.term: What ended mass Irish emigration to the USA
factCards.definition: The Great Depression after 1929 rather than the quotas; in the early 1930s more returned than left.

factCards.term: Commission on Emigration: dates and main finding
factCards.definition: Set up in 1948, reported in 1954; emigration was caused mainly by economic factors such as low incomes and lack of jobs.
About 400,000 left the state between 1951 and 1961, and the 1961 population fell to about 2.8 million.

factCards.term: Ellis Island: opening and first arrival
factCards.definition: Opened on 1 January 1892; the first person processed was Annie Moore from Cork.

factCards.term: Ireland Act 1949: Irish citizens in Britain
factCards.definition: Irish citizens in the United Kingdom were not treated as aliens and kept the right to live, work and vote there.

factCards.term: Post-war jobs of Irish emigrants in Britain
factCards.definition: Men on building sites, roads and power stations; women in nursing in the National Health Service and in factories.
About as many women as men left, unusual in Europe, and in some decades women outnumbered men.
Abolished national-origins quotas from 1968 in favour of family and skills, making entry harder for Irish without US relatives.
Essays edited by John A. O'Brien warning that emigration and late marriage were causing the Irish nation to die out.
